cur:monumental2-tokali-crucifixion.summary: In the conch of the main apse of the New Church, Christ hangs on a tall cross against a deep blue sky, his head bowed and his body slack in death, between the grieving Virgin and Saint John; the soldiers with lance and sponge and further mourners stand below, and angels and the sun and moon appear above the arms of the cross. Placing the Crucifixion directly over the altar, rather than a majestic Christ, made the sacrifice commemorated at every liturgy the visual centre of the church.
facts: The New Church was cut out of the east wall of the earlier Old Church and is famous for its intense blue backgrounds, painted with costly ultramarine made from lapis lazuli.

An inscription in the north apse names a painter, Nikephoros, and the patrons Constantine and his son Leo; Ann Wharton Epstein argued that Nikephoros' workshop was responsible for the whole decoration of the New Church.

cur:monumental2-tokali-crucifixion.notes: Dating of the New Church varies in the literature from the mid-10th century (Epstein: 'tenth-century metropolitan art') to the end of the 10th or early 11th century.

cur:objects3-sancta-sanctorum-staurothek.summary: This small wooden reliquary for a fragment of the True Cross has a cross-shaped cavity, around which are painted on gold the half-figure of Christ holding a book, the Virgin turned towards him with hands raised in prayer, two archangels, and full-length figures of Saints Paul and Peter, named in Greek. The Virgin's gesture of intercession towards her Son gives the little box the sense of a prayer gathered around the relic of the Cross.
facts: The inside of the sliding lid is painted with St John Chrysostom, and its outer face with a Crucifixion that is not visible in this photograph.
It came to the Vatican Museums from the papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum at the Lateran.

Q2653851.summary: Across the central panel, a team of straining, muscular men heaves the cross upright on a steep diagonal, while Christ, pale and luminous, lifts his eyes to heaven. The wings extend the drama: the Virgin, Saint John and mourning women at left, Roman officers and the two thieves at right. Painted soon after Rubens returned from some eight years in Italy, it fused the lessons of ancient sculpture, Michelangelo, Tintoretto and Caravaggio into a new, overwhelmingly physical Baroque language.
facts: The triptych was painted for the high altar of Saint Walburga's Church in Antwerp; because that church had fallen into ruin and was later demolished, the painting was placed in the cathedral after its return from France.
French revolutionary troops carried the painting to Paris in 1794, together with Rubens's Descent from the Cross; it was returned to Antwerp at the end of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815.
It hangs in the cathedral alongside Rubens's Descent from the Cross; the two paintings famously inspire the boy Nello in the 19th-century novel A Dog of Flanders.

The composition borrows from Tintoretto's Crucifixion in the Scuola di San Rocco, Venice, while several figures draw on ancient sculptures such as the Laocoön, which Rubens had studied and drawn in Rome.
